humanities_role_explanation: The benchmark measures the LLMs' domain-specific linguistic and stylistic alignment, evaluating whether they can replicate fine-grained rhetorical profiles (fingerprints) within a computational stylistics and forensic linguistics framework.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text-only corpus consisting of transcript dialogues and generated spoken decision statements.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Generative impersonation and stylistic analysis based on eight linguistic dimensions: sentence complexity, lexical diversity, discourse markers, nominalizations, modals, pronoun usage, and legal jargon.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped strictly to speaker-specific rhetorical impersonation and style mimicry within legal transcripts (parole suitability hearings).

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and DeepSeek R1.

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses z-scores over normalized linguistic feature counts (sentence complexity, lexical diversity (MTLD), and frequency-based features) compared against original human benchmarks.

summary: The paper explores the capacity of LLMs to mimic human conversational monologue in a high-stakes legal setting (parole hearings) by prompting them with speaker-specific rhetorical fingerprints. Using the PSH v1.0 corpus, the authors extract stylistic signatures of human commissioners to guide generative LLMs, analyzing the limits of prompt-based style alignment. Their findings show that LLMs possess strong, immutable model-specific fingerprints that dominate over the prompted styles.
key_findings: All tested LLMs show a strong bias towards formal, written-style features (e.g., excessive lexical diversity, high sentence complexity, and frequent nominalizations) regardless of explicit style prompts. GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 share very similar, inherited rhetorical patterns, while DeepSeek R1 exhibits the highest complexity and jargon usage, consistently ignoring negative constraints.
facets_explanation: The reference decision statements are extracted from official transcripts of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, which represent pre-existing administrative metadata. Evaluating whether the model can generate the correct decision and rationale requires external knowledge of California state laws and parole guidelines not present in the interview transcript stimulus. The evaluation compares the statistical rhetorical properties of the generated text against a single original reference text per hearing, meaning plurality and annotator consensus are not addressed.
